chunks.title: CT: when and how
chunks.tldr: CT = bone, blood, metal. Best for fractures, calcification, metal IOFB (glass/wood/plastic harder), sinus disease, acute intracranial blood, TED, orbital cellulitis/abscess. Order a dedicated orbit study (head CT doesn't show orbits well) with axial + coronal + parasagittal, bone and soft-tissue windows. 1-mm cuts for optic canal/traumatic optic neuropathy and IOFB. Contrast helps cellulitis vs abscess (not mandatory). Never use CT to rule out globe rupture; never use plain films for fractures.
points: Contrast caution: renal failure, diabetes, CHF, myeloma, sickle cell, asthma, multiple allergies. Shellfish allergy is not a contraindication.
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.
CTA: very sensitive for aneurysm but iodinated contrast + more radiation; prefer MRA in children.
ALARA: limit CT in children, but CT remains first choice for trauma at any age.
Plain X-ray only to screen for metal before MRI.
chunks.hook: CT: Calcium (bone), Clot (acute blood), Chunks of metal.

chunks.title: MRI, MRA, MRV & angiography
chunks.tldr: MRI = soft tissue: orbital apex, cavernous sinus, chiasm, nerve tumours, demyelination. Sequences: T1 fat bright, vitreous dark; T1 fat-sat + gadolinium (always for orbits — otherwise lesions vanish in fat); T2 fluid bright, melanin dark; FLAIR for MS plaques; DWI for stroke/lymphoma. Bright on T1 before gad: fat, mucus/protein (dermoid, mucocele), melanin, subacute blood (3–14 d), Aspergillus. MRA (no gad): aneurysm >2 mm, dissection. MRV: venous sinus thrombosis — all bilateral disc swelling. Catheter angiography: gold standard; stroke risk 0.3–1.8%; avoid in dissection.
points: Contraindications: some pacemakers, metallic IOFB, cochlear/stapes, nerve stimulators; titanium and gold lid weights are safe.
Gadolinium in renal failure → nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
Use closed high-field scanners for orbits.
Give the radiologist the clinical history (missed PComm aneurysms).
chunks.hook: Orbit MRI = T1 + fat-sat + gadolinium, every time.

cards.q: Name three lesions bright on T1 before gadolinium.
cards.a: Fat (lipoma/dermoid), melanin (melanoma), subacute blood; also mucus/protein and Aspergillus.

cards.q: Why is MRI contraindicated with an unknown IOFB?
cards.a: A ferromagnetic foreign body can move and cause further injury.

chunks.title: A-scan, B-scan, UBM & Doppler
chunks.tldr: A-scan: axial length for IOL (eyes within 0.3 mm), tumour reflectivity (standardised), congenital glaucoma follow-up; K readings before or 30 min after. B-scan: see through opacities — RD vs PVD (dynamic), choroidals (serous vs haemorrhagic), tumours, IOFB, occult posterior rupture, disc drusen, posterior scleritis (T-sign), screen blind eyes before evisceration. In trauma: over closed lids, no pressure; known rupture = relative contraindication. UBM (50–100 MHz): angle, ciliary body, plateau iris, cysts, cyclodialysis, IOL position. Orbital Doppler: reversed SOV flow (CCF), varix, CRAO/GCA flow.

cards.a: T-sign (fluid in sub-Tenon space around the optic nerve).

chunks.title: Fluorescein & ICG angiography
chunks.tldr: FA: excite 465–490 nm, emit 520–530; 80% protein bound; blocked by RPE and retinal capillary tight junctions. Phases: choroidal (8–15 s) → arterial → AV → venous (AV transit <11 s) → recirculation → late (10–30 min). Hyper: leakage (grows, e.g. CNV, CME), staining (fixed, scar), pooling (space, PED/CSCR), window defect (early, stable, RPE atrophy), autofluorescence (drusen). Hypo: blockage (blood, pigment) or non-perfusion. Side effects: nausea 10%, vomiting, urticaria; death ~1 in 220,000; yellow urine. ICG: infrared 805/835 nm, 95% bound, sees choroid through blood/pigment — PCV, occult CNV, RAP, CSCR, birdshot; iodine-based, liver excreted.
points: FAF: RPE health, AMD, dystrophies, HCQ, nevus orange pigment.
chunks.hook: Leak grows, pool fills a space, stain sits still, window shows early.

cards.q: Window defect vs leakage on FA?
cards.a: Window: early hyperfluorescence that stays same size/brightness (RPE atrophy). Leakage: increases in size and intensity over time.

cards.q: Why does ICG show the choroid better than fluorescein?
cards.a: Infrared fluorescence penetrates pigment, blood and fluid; high protein binding keeps it in choroidal vessels.

chunks.title: OCT, confocal & topography
chunks.tldr: OCT: light echo (~820 nm posterior, 1310 nm anterior), ~3 µm resolution; brightest layers RNFL and RPE; fluid dark. Uses: ME, CNV, CSCR, holes/ERM/VMT, RNFL/GCL in glaucoma, disc swelling/drusen. EDI for choroid; swept-source deeper; OCT-A = dye-free vessels (small field, needs fixation). HRT (confocal SLO): disc topography. Confocal microscopy: Acanthamoeba cysts, fungal hyphae, endothelial counts. Topography/tomography (Placido, Scheimpflug): keratoconus (posterior elevation), PMD, refractive screening, ectasia progression.
